name: Whirlpool Galaxy
description: A grand-design spiral locked in a slow gravitational dance with its smaller companion, NGC 5195. Its arms are some of the clearest examples of spiral structure in the sky.
humanFact: The light hitting your eyes tonight left this galaxy about 31 million years ago, long before humans existed.

name: NGC 1300
description: A large barred spiral galaxy seen nearly face-on. Its central bar funnels gas toward the galaxy's core, feeding new star formation along the way.
humanFact: The bar of stars across its middle is funneling gas toward the galaxy's core, the way water spirals toward a drain.

name: Virgo A
description: A giant elliptical galaxy at the heart of the Virgo Cluster, home to a jet of plasma thousands of light-years long and the supermassive black hole first imaged directly by the Event Horizon Telescope.
humanFact: At its center sits the black hole from the first photograph ever taken of one — you're seeing the galaxy, not the hole itself.

name: Needle Galaxy
description: One of the sky's most striking edge-on spirals, sliced through the middle by a thin, dark dust lane.
humanFact: This galaxy is a full-sized spiral like our own, just turned almost exactly edge-on, so it reads as a thin blade of light.

name: Antennae Galaxies
description: Two spiral galaxies caught mid-collision, their stars flung into long tidal tails that give the pair its name. A preview of what may lie ahead for the Milky Way and Andromeda.
humanFact: These two galaxies have been slowly colliding for hundreds of millions of years, and have hundreds of millions more to go.

name: Sombrero Galaxy
description: A nearly edge-on spiral with an unusually large central bulge and a sharp, dark dust lane, giving it the silhouette of a wide-brimmed hat.
humanFact: The dark band across its middle is a ring of dust wide enough to swallow thousands of solar systems.

name: NGC 891
description: An edge-on spiral often called a near-twin of the Milky Way as it might look from far away, complete with a dust lane knotted by star-forming clouds.
humanFact: If you could see the Milky Way from far outside it, it might look almost exactly like this.

name: Bode's Galaxy
description: A grand-design spiral and one of the closest large galaxies to the Milky Way, gravitationally bound to its turbulent neighbor M82.
humanFact: This is one of the closest large galaxies to our own — close enough that its gravity is slowly reshaping its neighbor.

name: Cigar Galaxy
description: A starburst galaxy undergoing an intense burst of star formation, likely triggered by its close pass with M81. Outflows of hot gas stream from its disc.
humanFact: A close pass with its neighbor M81 set off a burst of star formation so violent that gas is still blasting outward today.

name: Pinwheel Galaxy
description: A large, face-on spiral with sweeping, asymmetric arms studded with star-forming regions, likely shaped by past gravitational interactions.
humanFact: This galaxy's arms are lopsided, likely stretched out of shape by a smaller galaxy passing too close.

name: Fireworks Galaxy
description: A face-on spiral nicknamed for the unusually high number of supernovae observed within it over the past century.
humanFact: Astronomers have watched ten stars explode in this one galaxy over the last century alone — an unusually high number.

name: Sculptor Galaxy
description: A dusty starburst spiral, one of the brightest galaxies in the sky outside the Local Group and a favorite target of southern-sky imaging surveys.
humanFact: This galaxy is forming new stars so fast that it outshines most others its size.

name: NGC 7331
description: Sometimes called a twin of the Milky Way in size and structure, this tilted spiral anchors a small group of more distant background galaxies nicknamed the Deer Lick Group.
humanFact: This galaxy is close to the same size and shape as the Milky Way — a mirror of home, 40 million years in the past.

name: Helix Nebula
description: One of the closest planetary nebulae to Earth, formed by a dying sun-like star shedding its outer layers into space.
humanFact: This is what a star like our Sun will look like in its final centuries, breathing its outer layers back into space.

name: Ring Nebula
description: A glowing shell of gas cast off by a dying star, forming the ring shape that made it one of the first planetary nebulae ever discovered.
humanFact: The star that made this ring is still there, a tiny white ember burning at the exact center.

name: Cat's Eye Nebula
description: A planetary nebula with an intricate, layered structure of shells and knots, thought to result from a complex history of outbursts from its central star.
humanFact: The layered shells around this dying star record repeated outbursts, like rings written in light instead of wood.

name: Dumbbell Nebula
description: One of the brightest planetary nebulae in the sky, its double-lobed shape formed as a dying star's outer layers expanded outward in two directions.
humanFact: This is roughly what our own Sun will look like in about five billion years.

name: Skull Nebula
description: A planetary nebula with a mottled, uneven glow around a central pair of stars, giving it a hollow, skull-like appearance in deep images.
humanFact: Two faint stars orbit each other at the center of this cloud, all that remains of a star that once shone like the Sun.

name: M106
description: A spiral galaxy whose central supermassive black hole was one of the first to have its mass precisely measured, using water masers orbiting the galaxy's core.
humanFact: Astronomers measured the mass of this galaxy's black hole by tracking gas orbiting it at over a million miles per hour.

name: 3C 273
description: The first quasar ever identified, and one of the brightest, powered by a supermassive black hole devouring matter at the center of a distant galaxy.
humanFact: This single point of light outshines its entire host galaxy, powered by a black hole billions of times heavier than the Sun.

name: M77
description: A nearby spiral galaxy with an actively feeding supermassive black hole at its core, making it one of the closest and most studied Seyfert galaxies.
humanFact: Somewhere in this galaxy's bright core, matter is being pulled apart and swallowed right now.

name: NGC 5548
description: A well-studied Seyfert galaxy whose actively accreting black hole has been monitored for decades to trace the structure of gas swirling near its event horizon.
humanFact: Astronomers have been watching this galaxy's black hole flicker and feed for more than forty years.

name: M87
description: Home to M87*, the first black hole ever directly imaged, by the Event Horizon Telescope in 2019. The galaxy's relativistic jet spans thousands of light-years.
humanFact: The black hole itself is invisible — what you're looking at is the galaxy and glowing matter swirling around it.

name: Mice Galaxies
description: A pair of colliding spiral galaxies stretched into long, thin tidal tails by their mutual gravity, resembling two mice with long tails.
humanFact: Each galaxy has flung a long tail of stars out behind it, torn loose by the other's gravity.

name: Cartwheel Galaxy
description: A galaxy with a bright outer ring and a small compact core, likely the result of a smaller galaxy punching straight through its disc and sending ripples outward.
humanFact: This ring formed when a smaller galaxy punched straight through the middle of a larger one, like a stone dropped in a pond.

name: Hoag's Object
description: One of the most perfectly circular ring galaxies known, with a nearly complete ring of young blue stars surrounding an older yellow core, separated by a gap of nearly empty space.
humanFact: For over seventy years, astronomers have debated why this galaxy is such a near-perfect circle.

name: Einstein Cross
description: A single distant quasar appears four times around a much closer foreground galaxy, its light bent into a cross shape by gravitational lensing.
humanFact: This light left its source before the Sun existed, then got bent four separate ways around a closer galaxy on its way to you.

name: Arp 220
description: The closest ultraluminous infrared galaxy to Earth, formed by the ongoing merger of two spiral galaxies and glowing brightly from a burst of buried star formation.
humanFact: Two galaxies are merging here so violently that most of the collision is hidden behind a wall of dust.

name: Stephan's Quintet
description: A tight visual grouping of five galaxies, four of which are locked in a slow, repeated series of close encounters, distorting each other's spiral arms.
humanFact: Four of these five galaxies have been slowly colliding with each other for hundreds of millions of years.
